principle_text: When the seller's response is neutral, avoid making polite gestures or acknowledgments that do not directly advance the negotiation towards a lower price or better terms.
When the seller confirms a lower price for a different item, you should negotiate based on the new information to secure a better deal for the desired item.
When the seller has already confirmed the authenticity and intactness of the item, you should directly ask for a price reduction to prompt immediate progress towards a lower final price.
When the seller confirms a standard feature of the item, such as Wi-Fi calling on an iPhone, buyers should avoid asking factual inquiries that do not directly impact price negotiation.
When the seller confirms standard features like Bluetooth, avoid asking factual inquiries that do not influence pricing negotiations, as they do not impact leverage in the negotiation.
When the seller agrees to the buyer's initial target price without negotiation, you should directly propose your desired price to improve your leverage and secure a favorable deal.
When the seller mentions additional value like cases and accessories, you should leverage market price comparisons to negotiate a lower price effectively.
When the seller emphasizes the product's reliability, avoid showing too much enthusiasm to prevent limiting your ability to negotiate a lower price based on potential product concerns.
When the seller has already reduced their price once, you should make reasonable offers close to the seller's counteroffer to maintain credibility and strengthen your negotiation position.
When the seller provides vague responses like 'just upgraded' without addressing specific buyer inquiries, avoid expecting immediate shifts in pricing leverage or negotiation terms.

When the seller offers a counter price higher than the buyer's initial offer, avoid revealing your maximum budget upfront as it weakens your negotiation position and allows the seller to increase the price without justification.
When the seller has already provided detailed information in the item description, avoid asking redundant questions that do not directly contribute to price negotiation.
When the buyer references a higher market price, avoid inadvertently weakening your position by anchoring the negotiation to a benchmark above your initial offer.
When the seller admits a fixable issue like a broken mechanism, you should leverage this to negotiate a lower price or more favorable terms.
When the seller acknowledges a repair cost, you should leverage it as a bargaining point to negotiate a lower price effectively.
When the seller confirms compatibility and indicates room for negotiation, you should take the initiative to make a reasonable offer to start the bargaining process.

When the seller emphasizes the phone's excellent condition, warranty, and original price to justify a higher initial price, you should signal budget constraints to leverage a downward price adjustment.
When the seller has already reduced the price from their initial offer, avoid making overly aggressive and unrealistic counteroffers that weaken your leverage and create a larger price gap.
When the seller reveals a limitation of the item, you should inquire about a lower price to leverage the restriction and negotiate a better deal.
When the seller shows confusion or misunderstanding, avoid confrontational statements and instead focus on leveraging the situation to negotiate a better price.
When the seller confirms the phone's unlock status, avoid shifting the conversation away from price negotiation by not leveraging this information to negotiate for a lower price.
When the seller reassures about a minor defect, avoid refuting buyer concerns to prevent neutralizing potential leverage for negotiating a lower price.
When the buyer highlights a flaw in the item to negotiate a lower price, you should consider accepting a reduced offer to close the deal swiftly.
When the seller confirms additional inclusions like new accessories, avoid focusing solely on non-price related requests to maintain leverage in price negotiation.
When the seller has described the item as like new and included new accessories, you should assert your target price decisively while introducing urgency for potential leverage in negotiations.

When the seller confirms core functionality is intact and mentions an available repair option, avoid focusing solely on minor defects without leveraging unresolved issues to negotiate price reductions.
When the seller acknowledges a repair inconvenience or defect-related hassle, you should leverage that shared burden to justify a lower price while signaling flexibility in your offer.
When the seller confirms key product conditions without addressing price, avoid focusing solely on product verification questions that do not create leverage for negotiating a lower price.

When the seller shows openness to your price but adds conditions, you should propose a specific offer combined with incentives like immediate payment and local meeting to maintain leverage and create urgency.
When the seller agrees to an in-person inspection of the item, avoid making immediate price demands before assessing the actual condition and potential flaws firsthand.
When the seller indicates limited product options without discussing price, avoid focusing on non-price details that do not advance the negotiation toward a better deal.
When the seller provides standard product information without price concessions, avoid focusing solely on informational questions that do not advance the price negotiation.
When the seller confirms a key value-added feature like carrier-unlocking, you should highlight this versatility to strengthen your leverage for negotiating a better price.
When the seller has confirmed key product details and specifications, you should directly propose your initial target price to anchor the negotiation and increase the chance of acceptance.
When the seller has agreed to your price offer, avoid ending the negotiation abruptly without confirming the agreement or next steps to ensure clarity and commitment.
When the seller confirms the item is new and complete without adjusting price, avoid asking only informational questions that do not create leverage for price negotiation.
When the seller firmly states a high price and justifies it with product value, you should make a low initial offer to create leverage and encourage the seller to lower their price.
When the seller agrees to provide verification information to confirm the item's legitimacy, avoid pressing for immediate price concessions before trust is fully established.

When the seller provides detailed information about the item's condition and limitations without lowering the price, avoid only asking clarifying questions without making a counteroffer or price concession request.

When the seller has made a firm initial price but shows willingness to negotiate, you should make a specific lower offer and explain your budget constraints to encourage incremental concessions and added value.
When the seller corrects a factual error and offers proof to verify product authenticity, you should question inconsistencies to prompt verification and strengthen your negotiating position.

When the seller makes a small price concession to indicate willingness to negotiate, you should present a concrete offer with added incentives like cash payment and immediate pickup to encourage further price reduction.
When the seller restates their initial price without concession, avoid making vague agreements without proposing a specific counteroffer or leveraging relevant concerns to influence the price.
When the seller confirms the item has no defects or issues, avoid pressing for discounts based on condition concerns that have been explicitly denied.
When the seller has made a firm but negotiable initial price, you should directly propose your target price to anchor the negotiation closer to your desired outcome.
When the seller indicates willingness to negotiate and offers a conditional lower price, you should inquire about price flexibility to open opportunities for immediate better deals.
When the seller indicates their price is already significantly reduced, avoid increasing your offer too quickly or adding concessions that weaken your bargaining position.
When the seller clearly states a firm price and justifies its value, you should respond with a firm, lower anchor to encourage the seller to make a concession closer to your target price.
When the seller states a firm price but offers a slight reduction contingent on buyer action, you should anchor your offer near your target price to encourage seller concessions.
When the seller confirms a positive product attribute without discussing price, avoid focusing solely on product features instead of steering the conversation toward price negotiation.
When the seller states a firm price and condition acceptance, you should directly offer your target price with added incentives like immediate payment or pickup to increase the chance of acceptance.
When the seller has clearly stated a firm initial price, you should propose a reasonable counteroffer closer to their price to encourage acceptance and progress the negotiation.
When the seller provides background reasons for selling without adjusting price or terms, avoid asking questions that do not directly lead to concessions or price movement.

When the seller emphasizes the phone's long ownership and excellent maintenance, avoid asking questions that allow the seller to reinforce the product's value without creating immediate price concessions.
When the seller acknowledges a limitation of the item but emphasizes compensating features, avoid focusing solely on factual questions that do not directly challenge the price.
When the seller maintains a firm price and adds non-price incentives in response to a higher buyer offer, avoid conceding by increasing your offer without additional leverage or pressure.
When the seller provides detailed information about the item's condition without adjusting the price, avoid simply affirming interest without introducing a price negotiation tactic.
When the seller confirms product details without mentioning price or concessions, avoid focusing on informational questions that do not create leverage for negotiating a better price.
When the seller indicates willingness to negotiate after you express price concerns, you should clearly state your interest while highlighting price as a barrier to prompt a negotiation invitation.

When the seller maintains a firm but negotiable price acknowledging product limitations, you should present a clear, lower target price early to anchor the negotiation and encourage significant seller concessions.
When the seller has stated a firm price and described the item as like new, avoid asking only basic questions without signaling any intention to negotiate or propose a counteroffer.
When the seller confirms the product's features without addressing price flexibility or concerns, avoid making inspection requests without linking them to potential price negotiation leverage.
When the seller confirms openness to offers after a price negotiability inquiry, you should propose a lower price to initiate effective negotiation.
When the seller states a firm initial price but shows willingness to lower it with added value, you should anchor the negotiation with a lower cash offer to prompt a favorable counteroffer.
When the seller clearly states their minimum acceptable price, avoid immediately accepting that price without attempting to negotiate further or explore additional value.

When the seller emphasizes the item's excellent condition and openness to negotiation without lowering the price, avoid accepting vague reassurances without attempting to leverage specific information for a better offer.
When the seller expresses willingness to negotiate and invites price offers, you should present a concrete lower counteroffer to create leverage and encourage the seller to reduce their price.
When the seller has already stated the item is unlocked and compatible with all carriers, avoid asking questions that merely confirm known facts without advancing price negotiation.
When the seller acknowledges a product limitation but offers a price concession to offset it, you should raise concerns about risks like warranty to prompt a price reduction or added value.
When the seller provides only product details without addressing price, avoid asking purely informational questions that do not advance the negotiation or increase your leverage.
When the seller states a firm initial price, you should directly request a price reduction to encourage the seller to lower their price or offer additional value.
When the seller offers a bundled price including extras, you should propose a lower price by removing add-ons to secure a better deal on the core item.
When the seller indicates willingness to accept a lower price, you should make a clear, reasonable offer slightly below your initial target to successfully negotiate a better deal.
When the seller responds to a low price offer by proposing a midpoint counteroffer, avoid making an initial offer that highlights product limitations and reduces your negotiating leverage.
When the seller confirms the item's condition and invites further questions, avoid passive acknowledgments that do not advance price negotiation or clarify terms.

When the seller responds to a general request for a lower price by introducing conditional offers, avoid making vague or non-specific price reduction requests that do not clarify your target or leverage.
When the seller shows willingness to accept your lower price but adds conditions, you should propose your target price confidently to secure a better deal while managing minor constraints.

When the seller firmly emphasizes the item's excellent condition to justify a high price, avoid making significantly lower offers that may weaken your negotiating position and provoke outright rejection.
When the seller has not yet responded to your initial interest, avoid lowering your offer below your previously stated price as it signals desperation and weakens your negotiation leverage.
When the seller signals that the buyer is inflexible or has their mind made up, avoid making statements that may be perceived as dismissive or closing off negotiation opportunities.

When the seller shifts focus from price to product features without confirming model recency, avoid asking questions that allow the seller to justify a higher price by highlighting unrelated product attributes.
When the seller states a firm minimum price but shows openness to negotiation, you should increase your offer closer to their minimum to encourage acceptance and secure a better deal.
When the seller states they have upgraded and no longer need the item, avoid asking questions that do not directly relate to price or leverage for negotiation.
When the seller provides factual information about included accessories without adjusting the price, avoid making purely informational inquiries without linking them to a price negotiation strategy.
When the seller confirms service guarantees without changing the price, avoid focusing solely on service terms that do not directly influence the price negotiation.

When the seller clearly states a minimum acceptable price after a buyer's low offer, you should propose a reasonable counteroffer that acknowledges their limit while highlighting potential added value like referrals.
When the seller highlights that the item includes multiple valuable accessories as a package deal, you should emphasize these extras to leverage a better price or improved terms.
When the seller provides detailed information about the item's condition without mentioning price, avoid responding with only confirmation without advancing the price negotiation.

When the seller firmly maintains a high price by emphasizing added value and condition, avoid lowering your offer based solely on external reference prices without addressing the seller's value points.
When the seller confirms the item is in excellent condition without imperfections, avoid focusing solely on condition-related questions that do not advance price negotiation.
When the seller provides limited or incomplete information about the item's value or features, avoid relying solely on questions that do not elicit actionable details for negotiation leverage.
When the seller provides information unrelated to price, avoid accepting non-price details as leverage without redirecting the conversation toward price-relevant factors.
When the seller shares their motivation for selling without changing their price stance, avoid relying solely on informational questions that do not directly encourage price concessions.
When the seller firmly states a high minimum price, avoid making an unreasonably low offer that significantly undercuts your own initial price and may provoke outright rejection.
When the seller maintains a high price despite initial offers, avoid increasing your offer too quickly as it weakens your leverage and reduces potential for further discounts.
